title: Tetzaveh: holy on the forehead (Exodus 28:36–38)
hook: a gold plate on his forehead reads "HOLY TO THE LORD"

segments.voice: Yesterday, two stones on the high priest's shoulders and twelve on his chest, each one carrying a tribe's name. Your line was names on the heart. Whose name did you carry? Day three hundred sixty-two.

Where do you put the thing you most need to remember? A sticky note on the bathroom mirror. A word on your phone's lock screen. A string around a finger, if you're old enough to have tried it. People put reminders where their eyes will land. The Torah puts one somewhere the wearer can never see it at all. In this week's portion, Tetzaveh, the high priest's outfit gets one striking piece: a small plate of pure gold, tied across his forehead with a blue cord. Engraved on it, just two Hebrew words. Everyone who looks at him can read it. He can't.
screen: `A NOTE ON THE MIRROR.` → `A GOLD PLATE ON THE FOREHEAD.` → `EVERYONE CAN READ IT BUT HIM.`

segments.voice: The plate is called the tzitz, from a root that seems to mean a blossom or a shining thing. Exodus says to engrave it like a seal, and the words on it, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, are these: "HOLY TO THE LORD." The translators even print it in capital letters, the way an engraving would look. Then comes a strange line. The plate shall be on Aaron's forehead, the text says, and Aaron shall bear the iniquity of the holy things, the gifts the people bring, so that they may be accepted. It shall be always upon his forehead. So the plate does work. It carries the mistakes people make even in their offerings, and it has to stay put. The rabbis asked why the forehead, of all places. In the Talmud, each priestly garment is linked to a different kind of wrong it helps atone for, and the forehead plate is linked to brazenness. In Hebrew, a shameless person is called hard of forehead, the way English says someone has a nerve or a thick skin. The plate sits right on the spot where nerve lives, and covers it with holiness. And there's that detail from the hook: the priest can't read his own forehead. The words face out. Perhaps holiness worn on the face is mostly for the people you meet. They read it in how you look at them, long before you notice it yourself. Tetzaveh means you shall command, and here the command is that the most important words a person carries sit where everyone else can see them.
screen: `THE TZITZ: A PLATE OF PURE GOLD.` · `HOLY TO THE LORD.` · `HARD OF FOREHEAD: BRAZENNESS.` · `THE WORDS FACE OUT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one word to guide your thinking today. Settle, and breathe. Let a few words come up: gentle, honest, patient, careful, brave. Pick the one you need most. If you have paper, write it down. If not, trace it with a finger on your palm. Then touch your forehead lightly, as if you're placing it there. You won't see it all day. The people around you might. Breathe with it until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Tetzaveh. You shall command. The portion that dresses the high priest, ending with a gold plate on his forehead: holy to the Lord.
Your line: holy on the forehead. Today, before a hard conversation, touch your forehead once and remember your word. Day three hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Tetzaveh is read in synagogue in late winter, and the description of the high priest's garments, including the gold forehead plate, is studied each year as part of the weekly portion.

fork.reveal: on his forehead, on a gold plate: holy to the Lord. the words face everyone he meets, and never him.

original.note: Hebrew: holy to the Lord, the engraving on the gold plate. The divine name is read aloud as Adonai.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fancy gold ornament for a priest.
what it means: a plate engraved holy to the Lord, worn always, that carried the mistakes in the people's offerings.
what a scholar hears: the Talmud (Zevachim 88b) pairs each garment with a sin it atones for; the tzitz atones for brazenness, being hard of forehead.

notes: Exodus 28:36 'HOLY TO THE LORD' in JPS 1917 (printed in small capitals); confirm.
Zevachim 88b (and Arakhin 16a): the tzitz atones for brazenness (azut panim / 'hard of forehead'); confirm reference and phrasing.
Tzitz etymology as 'blossom / shining thing' is hedged ('seems to mean'); confirm or soften further.
The engraving, kodesh la-YHWH, is described as two Hebrew words; the Talmud (Shabbat 63b) discusses how it was laid out on the plate. Confirm the count.
The reading that the priest cannot see his own plate is a homiletic observation, not a classical source.
